source.title: Vector Quantized Latent Concepts: A Scalable Alternative to Clustering-Based Concept Discovery
source.authors: Xue-Min Yu; Ankur Garg; Samira Ebrahimi Kahou; Hassan Sajjad

record.tranche_reason: The paper evaluates pretrained SAE features and SAE-derived concept directions in LLM representations, including their activation rates and the effects of ablation on task predictions. This is a different method and measure from toy-model superposition studies.
record.gate_note: The paper mentions the superposition hypothesis as motivation for SAEs, but does not test toy-model superposition, capacity competition, feature geometry, or the claim that SAE features are canonical units. Rows below cover its own SAE-comparison results. Results comparing VQLC with clustering baselines are not included because those methods do not test the claim versions.
record.test_reason: This is a concept-discovery methods paper (VQLC vs K-Means and hierarchical clustering). Pretrained SAEs (Qwen-Scope, Gemma-Scope) are used only as a comparator to the authors' own method. The SAE results measure how much ablating SAE-derived directions changes classification outputs, and how often SAE units activate on test examples. None of this tests whether features are superposed, spread across neurons, or recoverable by a dictionary, nor whether SAE features are canonical units. Superposition is mentioned only as motivation for SAEs in Related Work.
record.authors_conclusion: Partly right. The main conclusion is that VQLC is a scalable alternative to clustering-based concept discovery: near-constant memory, competitive faithfulness, best gains on decoder-only models. On SAEs, the authors say VQLC encodes more task-relevant information. They also say SAEs yield larger inventories with lower active rates, and that individual SAE features 'can perturb output in some cases'. They draw no conclusion about superposition.
record.recipe_differences: The study proposes vector-quantized concept discovery and compares pretrained SAE features using concept-direction projection and direct feature ablation; it does not reproduce the original toy-model superposition method.
record.method_sensitivity: Results vary by dataset, SAE assignment procedure (top1 versus top5), and model (Qwen versus Gemma).

fits_no_version.finding: For classification on Qwen3.5-2B and Gemma-3-4B-IT, ablating SAE-derived directions or features changes predictions little in many settings. SAE units are active on a minority of test examples, compared with a 400-code VQ codebook.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Individual SAE features/feature-averaged directions carry limited task-decision information at the classification token compared with task-level concept codebooks.

record.problems: The SAE comparison covers classification tasks and selected models/settings, not generative behavior or representation geometry. SAE feature impact is assessed through ablation; the paper does not establish that the SAE recovers complete or canonical underlying model features. The authors also note that the study focuses on classification tasks and that VQLC design choices require tuning.
record.rows_left_out: No rows omitted. The paper also reports VQLC results and comparisons with clustering baselines, which do not bear directly on the listed claim versions.

untested.parts: No toy models, sparsity sweep, or geometry.
No measure of features spread across neurons, and no test of whether SAEs recover sparse model features. SAEs are used off the shelf.
No test of completeness, stability or canonicity of SAE features.

record.verdict_notes: Reclassified from tests/T2 to uses_without_test/T4. The SAE results are comparator baselines for the authors' own method, not a test of any superposition version. Record labels removed. The record also swaps ERASER and Jigsaw for the Qwen SAE-concept rows (Table 3 vs Table 14) and likely for the Gemma rows (Table 16 ordering plus the authors' 'ERASER exception' remark).

versions.untested_parts: No toy networks, feature-over-dimension sweep, sparsity transition, or feature geometry is tested.
No capacity competition, dedicated dimensions, or polysemanticity is tested.
No alternative causes of polysemanticity are tested.

The paper evaluates pretrained SAE features and their effects in classification settings, but does not test whether features are spread across neurons, whether the SAE recovered the model's underlying features, or feature recovery stability.
The paper does not test whether SAE features are complete, stable, or canonical units.
No comparison of one-dimensional versus multidimensional features or feature geometry is made.
